extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school and undergraduate students, contest/problem-solving readers studying classical Euclidean geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of solution strategies, hints and short proofs for a broad set of classical Euclidean geometry problems (construction, inequality, extremal, covering, combinatorial geometry). Useful for contest preparation and self-study.

rubrics_metrics.name: construct_regular_tetrahedron_and_cones
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose the source of light is in O. We construct a regular tetrahedron ABCD with center O. Consider the four infinite circular cones, each containing strictly the four pyramids OBCD, OACD, OABC, OABD and common vertex O.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetric construction (regular tetrahedron) about a central point to reduce 3D visibility/covering problems to cone problems; inscribe spheres into the cones (with carefully chosen radii) so that every ray from O intersects some sphere. Example: shows why four equal spheres cannot shield the light and suggests minimal number/radius considerations (six equal spheres needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: use_specific_slot_constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: For cutting problems, use purpose-shaped slots: an H-shaped slot will do for (a) and a T-shaped slot for (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design explicit auxiliary cutouts (H or T shapes) to realize required separations/reconstructions; these are concrete constructive hints rather than general existence proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: reflect_triangles_to_partition_hexagon
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect the triangles A1A2A6, A2A3A4, and A4A5A6 at their bases, and you get a partition of the hexagon into three rhombi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflections across sides/bases to transform a polygon into symmetric parts (rhombi) and deduce angle equalities or other structural properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: reflect_curve_at_origin_to_find_chord_through_origin
rubrics_metrics.description: If O ∉ C, reflect C at O to C'. If C ∩ C' ≠ ∅ then pick A ∈ C ∩ C' and B its reflection at O; AB passes through O.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflecting whole curves about a point can force intersections and give existence of chords/lines through the center; use symmetry of the reflected image to conclude passes through O.

rubrics_metrics.name: arrange_alternating_sums_to_prove_divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that n must be a multiple of 8 (or 12) by grouping integers into alternating-signed blocks whose sums vanish: (1−3−5+7)+(9−11−13+15)+⋯ = 0 etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create blockwise telescoping/alternating-sum groupings to exhibit modular or divisibility constraints. Compose explicit sequences whose block sums are zero to prove sufficiency as well as necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: triangulation_counting_by_angle_sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose convex hull of N points is an r-gon. Sum of angles of all triangles in triangulation is 180°(r−2)+360°(N−r). Number of triangles is r−2+2(N−r)=2N−r−2, giving segment bounds 2N−3 ≤ s ≤ 3N−6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count triangles via global angle sum: first term from hull polygon, second term from interior points. Use double-counting of triangle sides to deduce counts/inequalities for segments and triangulation structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_area_ratio_relations
rubrics_metrics.description: From A1/A4 = A2/A3 one gets A1A2A3A4 = (A1A3)^2 (i.e., relations between products of areas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate equal area ratios into multiplicative relations among area terms to deduce equalities/inequalities of side-length or area products.

rubrics_metrics.name: centroid_permutation_invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S be the centroid of H and S' = f(S). But {A1',...,An'} is a permutation of H. Hence S = S'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use centroid linearity and invariance under permutation of same multiset of points to deduce fixedness or symmetry properties; useful when a mapping permutes vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: rotation_about_center_for_regular_polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: In a regular pentagon use rotation about its center by 72° to relate points Pi and Ai and interpret segments as vectors; O becomes the centroid of Pi etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit rotational symmetry (specific rotation angles for regular n-gons) to express distances/vectors and use triangle inequality or centroid arguments to derive bounds and equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: unit_sphere_dot_product_one-line_inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the unit sphere about O. |P Ai| = |Ai − P|·|Ai| ≥ (Ai − P)·Ai / |Ai| = Ai·Ai/|Ai| − P·Ai/|Ai| ≥ ... leading to a one-line solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vector dot-product inequalities on the unit sphere (or normalization) to obtain concise bounds; good for succinct proofs involving distances to several fixed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: ellipse_reflection_foci_property
rubrics_metrics.description: Since AB ∥ CD, C and D are reflections at the perpendicular bisector of AB. This follows from the construction of the ellipse with foci A, B and constant sum of distances |AC| + |BC| = |AD| + |BD| = 2a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflection properties of ellipses (sum of distances to foci constant) and perpendicular bisector symmetry to deduce reflection relations among points.

rubrics_metrics.name: minimal_enclosing_circle_symmetry_argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the smallest circle containing all points of S (largest of all circles through triples of points etc.). Any reflection at a perpendicular bisector leaves this circle fixed and hence passes through its center O; therefore all points are equidistant from O.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extremal (smallest enclosing circle) and symmetry under reflections to deduce that all boundary points are equidistant (i.e., lie on a circle). Note: fails for infinite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: isometry_rotation_argument_for_configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the lengths of sides a and the angle α are given for five points, then the figure is determined up to an isometry S that permutes vertices cyclically; S is a rotation fixing centroid, hence the points lie in a plane perpendicular to axis of rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use group/ isometry arguments: show permutations correspond to rotations or reflections, then use fixed-point properties (centroid fixed ⇒ rotation) to deduce planarity or other geometric constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: incircle_touchpoints_to_bound_segment_distance
rubrics_metrics.description: For convex ABCD, consider incircles of triangles ABC and CDA touching AC in T1 and T2. Prove |T1T2| ≥ (1/2)|(|AB|+|CD|)−(|BC|+|AD|)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare touchpoints of incircles on a shared diagonal to bound distances between touchpoints using side-length sums; apply in inequalities involving quadrilaterals.

rubrics_metrics.name: area_covering_via_partition_and_counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut up the yard into 50 strips of width 2. If the center of a barrel is outside a strip S then barrel has no point in common with its symmetry line; at most eight pieces remain uncovered etc. Hence at least 8·50=400 barrels inside the yard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition the domain into strips/regions and count uncovered/covered pieces with local bounds to derive global lower/upper bounds (packing/covering arguments). Useful for discrete geometry/packing problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: extremal_point_triangle_inequality_approach
rubrics_metrics.description: To find minimal distance sum from three points consider two cases: Fermat point with all angles <120° (use equilateral triangle construction), or the vertex with angle ≥120° is the minimizer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known extremal characterizations (Fermat point) and construct auxiliary equilateral triangles or perpendiculars; break into cases depending on largest angle to determine minimizer.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_parity_on_coordinate_differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Denote coordinate differences xi, yi which are integers with xi^2 + yi^2 = R. Use congruences mod 4 and parity of sums to deduce that n is even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply modular arithmetic (mod 2, mod 4) to integer coordinate differences and use parity counting to deduce global parity constraints on the number of sides/points.

rubrics_metrics.name: construct_triangle_from_side_angle_and_difference_of_other_sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce construction to known construction of triangle from one side, the opposite angle, and the difference of the remaining sides by marking off a segment AM = AB − BC on AD and constructing isosceles ACD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate a construction requirement into standard constructions (marking off segments equal to differences) and use classical triangle construction steps and circumcircle intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: box_through_corridor_conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A box with sides a ≤ b fits through a corridor with door dimensions c,d iff a ≤ c, a ≤ d, and ab ≤ cd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish necessary conditions by comparing smaller side to door widths and area/comparison using critical 'stuck' configuration; derive sufficiency by constructing the critical parallelogram/rectangle case.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_Heron_and_trigonometric_relations_to_test_right_triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce formulas 4AR = abc, A = sr, A^2 = s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c). Using 2R + r = s and algebraic rearrangement leads to (−a^2 + b^2 + c^2)(a^2 − b^2 + c^2)(a^2 + b^2 − c^2) = 0, which holds iff triangle is right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine classical area formulas and relations between inradius, circumradius, semiperimeter to derive algebraic conditions characterizing right triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: mass_point_assignment_for_coplanarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign masses 1/a,1/b,1/c,1/d to A,B,C,D so that centroids of pairs lie on chords RT and SU; intersection point is centroid of four vertices implying R,S,T,U are coplanar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mass-point (weighted centroid) assignments to show alignment/coplanarity of contact points between a quadrilateral and its circumscribed sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: apply_Pick_and_Heron_for_lattice_triangle_arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick's theorem with i + b/2 − 1 = area and Heron's formula combine to show that for a lattice triangle with no interior/boundary lattice points the side-squared relations force at least one lattice point on the sides or inside for acute triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix lattice-area relations (Pick) and classical continuous formulas (Heron) to get arithmetic constraints on side lengths that force combinatorial conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: circle_selection_scaling_argument_for_packing
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the circle of largest radius, blow it up by factor 3, remove all circles inside the blown-up circle and iterate; the original circles of 1/3 radius do not intersect and their common area > 1/9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iterative maximal-selection and scaling (blow-up) to extract disjoint families and lower-bound union area; standard in packing/covering estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: rotation_homothety_and_Appolonius_circle_for_construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rotational homothety with center A, angle α and factor d/a mapping B to D; locus for A includes circle about D radius a and Appolonius circle for ratio d:a. Intersections give construction points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine rotation+scaling (rotational homothety) with Apollonius circle loci to reduce quadrilateral construction to intersection of standard loci (circles, diameters).

rubrics_metrics.name: bisecting_planes_for_tetrahedron_incenter
rubrics_metrics.description: The three bisecting planes of a solid angle of a tetrahedron intersect in a line which is the locus of points equidistant from the faces; intersecting another bisecting plane yields center O equidistant from all four faces (insphere center).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plane-bisector intersection logic in 3D: bisector planes are loci equidistant from face pairs; their common intersection yields the center of the inscribed sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: trigonometric_optimization_for_shortest_path
rubrics_metrics.description: Model path length p(α,β)=2π + (1/cos α + tan α − 2α) + (tan β − 2β) and minimize separately in α,β; unique minima at α=π/6, β=π/4 giving minimal path length ≈ 6.397.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the parametric expression for path length using geometry/trig, separate variables when possible, analyze derivatives or sign changes to find unique minima for each variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: transformations_preserve_lines_and_circles_argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be any bijective transformation of the plane with a fixed point. Show inverse images of collinear points are collinear and images of collinear points are collinear by considering images of circles with diameters and touch properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use circle-image properties under bijections (circles map to circles; tangency preserved in image sense) and simple contradiction arguments to derive collinearity preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_Ptolemy_to_bound_segment_lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: From Ptolemy's theorem on quadrilateral cross-product relations derive e.g. |AA1|·|BC| = |AB|·|CA1| + |AC|·|BA1| and deduce lower bounds like |AA1| > (|AB|+|AC|)/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Ptolemy to cyclic quadrilaterals or use its inequality variants to bound distances from chord/subtended arcs; sum inequalities across vertices to get global perimeter bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: maximize_segment_via_diameter_choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Circle Z with diameter AP passes through M and N so |MN| is maximal when diameter AP is maximal (i.e., when P is antipodal of A); then |MN|max = |BC|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate a target segment to a chord/subtended chord of a circle with variable diameter; maximize diameter to maximize the chord length, reaching a concrete comparison with a fixed side.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_Jordan_inequality_for_sine_lower_bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Jordan's inequality 0<x<π/2 ⇒ sin x > 2x/π to show sums like a+b+c = 2r(sin α + sin β + sin γ) > 4r, giving perimeter > 4r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply classical inequalities (Jordan's, monotonicity of trig sums) to bound trigonometric expressions and convert to geometric inequalities about perimeters or areas.
